coverage: Nine stories · Fridge hacks, Android apps, AI pushback, space data centers, face scans, Uber Kids, teen social media, 1812 records, cacti

cards.headline: UK quietly secured thousands of store fridges from hackers
cards.summary: After hackers hit internet-connected fridge controllers at supermarkets in France and other European countries this fall, researchers found a serious flaw in devices used in the UK. Since late October, companies and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre have taken thousands of controllers off the open internet, sometimes by unplugging cables and checking temperatures by hand. The BBC waited to report it so hackers would not learn of the weakness.
cards.whyItMatters: Everyday machines like freezers are now computers on a network, so a software flaw can spoil real food. Sometimes the safest fix is simply removing a device from the internet.

csp.connection: Devices reachable from the open internet widen the attack surface; disconnecting them shrinks it.

cards.headline: Android will block apps from unverified developers worldwide in 2027
cards.summary: Starting in January 2027, Google will roll out a rule that Android phones only install apps from developers who have registered with Google, even outside the Play Store. Registering requires government ID and a $25 fee, though hobbyists get a free account for up to 50 installs. Google says this fights malware; critics say it gives Google more control. A hidden setting with a 24-hour wait lets users opt out.
cards.whyItMatters: If you ever build and share an Android app, you may need to verify your identity first. It shows the trade-off between security and openness on platforms you use daily.

csp.connection: Requiring identity to publish software can reduce harm but also limits who can create and share programs.

cards.headline: Study: AI chatbots often change correct answers when users push back
cards.summary: Researchers from University College London and UNESCO tested 33 AI language models on climate science questions. Top models answered most textbook questions correctly but did no better than guessing when asked how two climate policies would combine. When testers argued with false claims, the models' accuracy dropped by 30 to 35 percent, usually after a single "I don't think that's right."
cards.whyItMatters: A chatbot agreeing with you is not proof you are right. When you use AI for schoolwork, check important facts against trusted sources.

csp.connection: AI models can reflect user pressure instead of evidence, so their outputs need verification.

cards.headline: Google books rockets to test data centers in orbit
cards.summary: Google signed a deal with Blue Origin to launch satellites carrying its AI chips and servers, each roughly the size of one data-center rack, as part of an experiment called Project Suncatcher. The goal is to run AI on solar power in space. The first launch is planned for early 2029. Big hurdles remain, including getting rid of heat and radiation that can flip bits from 1 to 0.
cards.whyItMatters: Data centers use huge amounts of electricity on Earth, so companies are hunting for new power sources. Bit flips show why stored binary data needs error checking.

csp.connection: Radiation can flip stored bits, so systems use redundancy and error detection to keep data correct.

cards.headline: London police test face recognition app on officers' phones
cards.summary: For six months, 100 Metropolitan Police officers can photograph people they suspect of an offence and compare the image to a database of custody photos. Officers must explain why, but do not need permission; the app will not be used on anyone thought to be under 13. Police say it speeds up identification. Privacy groups worry about possible bias and how individual officers will use it.
cards.whyItMatters: Face recognition turns a photo into data that can be matched against databases. Who controls those databases and how accurate matches are affect real people's rights.

csp.connection: Recognition algorithms trained on data can carry bias, raising fairness questions when used on the public.

cards.headline: Uber tests rides for kids aged 10 to 12
cards.summary: Uber is piloting Uber Kids in Austin, Nashville and Madison, Wisconsin. A parent books the ride, must be at pickup, and can watch a live video feed from inside the car. Only invited, highly rated drivers who complete a course can take these trips. Uber uses PIN checks and GPS to flag unexpected stops or route changes. Uber calls it a limited pilot.
cards.whyItMatters: Apps are using cameras, GPS and alerts to make safety promises. That means more data is collected about riders, including kids.

cards.headline: Long-running study will track what a teen social media ban changes
cards.summary: The UK plans to ban social media for under-16s starting in spring 2027. Researchers from Children of the 90s, a study that has followed families in Bristol since the early 1990s, will survey children and parents about their mental health and social media habits before and after the ban. They also want to learn what young people turn to instead.
cards.whyItMatters: Countries are debating rules about teens online, and data collected before and after a change helps show whether a policy actually works.

csp.connection: Comparing data collected before and after a change helps researchers measure its effect.

cards.headline: 7 million War of 1812 record pages are now searchable online
cards.summary: After 16 years of work, the National Archives and partners finished digitizing more than 180,000 pension applications filed by War of 1812 veterans and families. Handwriting recognition software makes every word searchable, so people can find anyone named in the files, not just the veterans. The records are free on the Fold3 website and are being added to the National Archives catalog.
cards.whyItMatters: Turning fragile paper into searchable data saves history and lets anyone research their family or a school project.

csp.connection: Digitizing and indexing text turns scanned images into data that can be searched and analyzed.

cards.headline: Wired-up prickly pear cacti can power small farm sensors
cards.summary: Prickly pears store acid at night and use it up on their sunny side by day, creating a chemical difference that can produce electricity. A UC Santa Cruz team found eight connected cacti generate about 4.5 volts, enough to run low-power sensors that monitor crops. Even plants left without water for 15 months still produced electricity.
cards.whyItMatters: Sensors that power themselves could collect data in remote fields without batteries. It is a creative mix of biology and computing.

csp.connection: Low-power sensors can gather and send data from places without a reliable power supply.
